title: How Book Banning Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how book banning works in the United States. They preview Banned Books Week (late September/early October) and note that the American Library Association opposes censorship and holds a Library Bill of Rights stance on minors' access. A book is effectively "banned" when a single challenger convinces a librarian to remove it from a library, and the episode covers the frequency of challenges, commonly challenged books (The Catcher in the Rye, To Kill a Mockingbird, Harry Potter, Judy Blume, and others), and the legal history from Socrates and the Star Chamber through Island Trees v. Pico, Hazelwood v. Kuhlmeier, and the Miller test for obscenity. They also discuss the Texas textbook review committee and social studies curriculum revisions, and close with a listener mail segment about disco from Diane in Kentucky.
topics: Island Trees School District v. Pico

segments.title: Opening banter and Banned Books Week preview
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck banter about the episode's topic and about Banned Books Week, which falls in the last week of September or first week of October, and its purpose of celebrating intellectual freedom.

segments.title: Book challenges and The Catcher in the Rye
segments.summary: They note more than eleven thousand books have been challenged since 1982, including a teacher fired in 1960 for assigning The Catcher in the Rye. They discuss common reasons for challenges and recent examples such as The Hunger Games and Brave New World.

segments.title: American Library Association and Library Bill of Rights
segments.summary: The hosts explain that the American Library Association is a librarians' lobby opposed to censorship, not the body banning books, and describe its Library Bill of Rights stance that parents, not other people, decide what their own children read.

segments.title: How a book gets banned
segments.summary: A formal challenge is made to a single library and the librarian decides whether to remove the book, usually leaning toward keeping it. A book is effectively banned when one person convinces a librarian to remove it for everyone, often with group pressure, and courts usually defend the First Amendment.

segments.title: History of censorship from Socrates to Star Chamber
segments.summary: Historical overview: ancient attempts to suppress teachings such as burning copies (Socrates drank hemlock), the printing press making burning impractical, and the seventeenth-century English Star Chamber and Henry VIII's licensing laws allowing prepublication censorship.

segments.title: Island Trees v. Pico and Hazelwood cases
segments.summary: The Island Trees School District case held that school officials cannot remove library material merely because they disagree with ideas, with school libraries given special protection. The Hazelwood case limited the free-expression rights of high school newspapers, allowing schools to censor them and extending to classroom curriculum.
topics: Island Trees School District v. Pico

segments.title: Texas textbook review and obscenity law
segments.summary: Texas's influential, largely conservative textbook review committee sought social studies revisions starting around 2009, affecting national textbooks. Obscenity is excluded from First Amendment protection, tracing from the 1873 Comstock laws through Roth v. United States and the three-part Miller test, where the burden of proof lies on the challenger. The segment is cut off in the transcript with banned-book authors and a listener mail segment.
